questions.stem: Given a single point P, what shape forms the set of all points equidistant from P?
questions.solution: The set of all points equidistant from a single point forms a circle, where that point is the center. Therefore, the correct answer is C: A circle centered at P.
questions.explanation: Loci problems deal with sets of points satisfying certain geometric conditions. In this case, the condition is 'equidistant from P', which defines a circle.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake is to choose A (a line), assuming that equidistance would result in a straight line, but that's not true for all points; or D (a segment), which only considers two distances instead of all possible distances.

questions.stem: Given two distinct points A and B, what shape forms the set of all points that lie on the same line as A and B?

choices.A: A ray starting at A and passing through B
choices.B: A segment with endpoints A and B
choices.C: The union of a ray starting at A and a ray starting at B
choices.D: An infinite straight line passing through both A and B

questions.solution: The set of all points that lie on the same line as two distinct points forms an infinite straight line passing through both points. Therefore, the correct answer is D: An infinite straight line passing through both A and B.
questions.explanation: Loci problems can also involve lines defined by two or more points. In this case, since we're looking for a line, the set includes all points on that line, not just those between the two given points.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake is to choose B (a segment), which only considers the portion of the line between the two points; or C (union of two rays), which doesn't account for points beyond A and B on the same line.

questions.stem: Given a line segment AB, what shape forms the set of all points that are equidistant from both endpoints A and B?

choices.A: A ray starting at midpoint M of AB
choices.C: The altitude from point A to line AB
choices.D: The median from point A to line AB

questions.solution: The set of all points equidistant from the endpoints of a line segment forms its perpendicular bisector, which is a line perpendicular to the segment and passing through its midpoint. Therefore, the correct answer is B: The perpendicular bisector of AB.
questions.explanation: This problem involves finding the geometric locus for points that are equidistant from both endpoints of a line segment, which results in a specific type of line called the perpendicular bisector.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake is to choose A (a ray), which only considers one side of the midpoint; or C and D (altitudes and medians), which are related concepts but not the set of points equidistant from both endpoints.

questions.stem: Given a circle with center O, what shape forms the set of all points that form an inscribed angle with vertex at point P?

choices.A: A sector with central angle at P
choices.B: The arc of the circle subtended by the inscribed angle at P
choices.C: All points on the circle except for P itself

questions.solution: The set of all points that form an inscribed angle with vertex at a point on a circle is the arc of the circle subtended by that angle. Therefore, the correct answer is B: The arc of the circle subtended by the inscribed angle at P.
questions.explanation: In this problem, we're looking for the set of points that form an inscribed angle with vertex at point P on a circle, which corresponds to the portion of the circle's circumference defined by that angle.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake is to choose A (a sector), which includes the area inside the angle and not just the arc; or C (all points except P), which doesn't account for the arc formed by the inscribed angle; or D (the line segment OP), which is a chord of the circle, not the set of points forming an inscribed angle.

questions.stem: Given a triangle ABC, what shape forms the set of all points that lie on the circumference of the circle passing through A, B, and C?

choices.A: The intersection of the medians of triangle ABC
choices.B: The intersection of the altitudes of triangle ABC
choices.C: The intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of sides AB, BC, and CA
choices.D: The intersection of the angle bisectors of angles A, B, and C

questions.solution: The set of all points that lie on the circumference of a circle passing through the vertices of a triangle forms the circumcircle, which is defined by the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the triangle's sides. Therefore, the correct answer is C: The intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of sides AB, BC, and CA.
questions.explanation: This problem involves finding the geometric locus for points that lie on a circle passing through all vertices of a triangle, which is called the circumcircle and can be constructed using perpendicular bisectors.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake is to choose A (the intersection of medians), B (the intersection of altitudes), or D (the intersection of angle bisectors), which are related concepts but not the set of points lying on the circumcircle.

questions.stem: Given a triangle ABC, what shape forms the set of all points that divide each median into two segments with lengths in the ratio 2:1?

choices.B: The angle bisectors of angles A, B, and C
choices.C: The perpendicular bisectors of sides AB, BC, and CA

questions.solution: The set of all points that divide each median of a triangle into two segments with lengths in the ratio 2:1 is the centroid of the triangle. Therefore, the correct answer is D: The centroid of triangle ABC.
questions.explanation: This problem involves finding the geometric locus for points that bisect medians in a specific ratio, which turns out to be the centroid, a well-known point in any triangle.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake is to choose A (altitudes), B (angle bisectors), or C (perpendicular bisectors), which are related concepts but not the set of points dividing medians in a 2:1 ratio.

questions.stem: Given a parabola with focus F and directrix d, what shape forms the set of all points that are equidistant from both F and d?

choices.A: A line parallel to d passing through F
choices.B: The perpendicular bisector of the line segment connecting F and any point on d
choices.C: An infinite straight line passing through F and parallel to d
choices.D: A curve that is symmetrical about a vertical line passing through F

questions.solution: The set of all points in a plane that are equidistant from a fixed point (focus) and a fixed line (directrix) forms a parabola. Therefore, the correct answer is D: A curve that is symmetrical about a vertical line passing through F.
questions.explanation: This problem involves understanding the definition of a parabola as the set of points equidistant from a focus and a directrix, which results in a specific type of curve.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake is to choose A (a line parallel to d), which describes a different geometric figure; B (perpendicular bisector) and C (infinite straight line) are related concepts but not the set of points defining a parabola.
